title: The jewel in the coat (Kern ch. 8)
hook: a friend sews a jewel into a sleeping man's coat; he wanders poor for years without knowing

segments.voice: Yesterday, a worn-out caravan rested in a city their guide had conjured, and then he told them the treasure was further on. Your line: a city to rest in. Where did you rest, and did you get up again? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

A coat hangs by the door. Down in the lining, stitched where no hand goes looking, there's a jewel worth more than everything its owner will earn this year. He wears that coat to work every day. He counts coins at the end of every week. He never finds it. That's the whole parable, almost. What makes it strange is who tells it. In chapter eight of the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha has just promised a large company of monks that they too will one day be Buddhas. They don't answer with thanks. They answer with a story, and the story is about themselves. Today: the jewel in the coat.
screen: `A COAT BY THE DOOR.` → `A JEWEL IN THE LINING.` → `THE LISTENERS TELL THIS ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the story the monks tell. A man goes to visit a friend who is well off. There's food, there's drink, and the man falls asleep. The friend has to leave on business before his guest wakes. So, as a parting gift, he sews a priceless jewel into the sleeping man's garment, and goes. The man wakes up alone, wanders off to another country, and scrapes by. He works hard for food and clothes, and when he gets a little, he's satisfied with it. A long time later, the friend runs into him and is astonished. Why are you living like this? I gave you a jewel. It's in your coat. Look. Then the monks say what it means. We were that man. Long ago, they say, the Buddha placed in us the aim of full awakening. We slept through it. We found a small peace, a little rest, and we told ourselves it was the whole of it. Now he has shown us the lining. Notice the friend. He doesn't take the jewel back for being ignored. He doesn't wait for the man to deserve it. He just points. And this is the week's last day, so look at what the Lotus has been doing all week. A son who doesn't know he's the heir. Travelers resting in a city that isn't the end of the road. A man poor with a fortune stitched into his clothes. Three stories, one turn: what the searcher wants has already been handed over. Some later teachers read the jewel as buddha-nature, already present in everyone, waiting to be noticed. The sutra itself keeps the picture simple: a coat, a lining, a friend who says look.
screen: `THE MONKS TELL A STORY ON THEMSELVES.` · `A JEWEL SEWN IN WHILE HE SLEPT.` · `HE WANDERS, GLAD OF SCRAPS.` · `THE GIFT WAS THERE ALL ALONG.` · then, large: `THE JEWEL IN THE COAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: find one hidden gift. Settle, and let the breath come and go on its own. Feel the weight of whatever you're wearing, the cloth on your shoulders. This time, be the friend in the story. Bring to mind one person who seems to be getting by on scraps: someone who doubts themselves, or waves away what they're good at. Look for what's stitched into their lining: a steadiness, a kindness, a knack they never mention. Don't weigh whether it's big enough. Just find it, and hold it the way you'd hold something you mean to hand back. If nothing comes, rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The jewel in the coat. A gift sewn in while the man slept, carried for years without his knowing. Today's word.
screen: `THE JEWEL IN THE COAT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the jewel in the coat. Today, like the friend, point out one gift to someone who hasn't noticed it in themselves. The son, the city, the coat: that was the week. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, the jewel in the coat is taught alongside the lost son and the phantom city as one of the sutra's parables about a gift already given and not yet recognized.

fork.setup: you wake up alone in your friend's house. your friend is gone. what do you do?

original.note: Sanskrit: a jewel, a treasure. the same word names the Three Jewels, the triratna.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about bad luck and a lucky break.
what it means: a man lives poor with a priceless jewel sewn into his coat, and a friend finally shows him where it is.
what a scholar hears: in chapter eight the listeners answer the Buddha's promise with their own parable; some later teachers read the jewel as buddha-nature.

notes: Parable paraphrased from Kern (1884) ch. 8, not quoted (wording unverified). Check: guest falls asleep (Kern: after food/drink, some versions 'drunk'), friend leaves on business, jewel sewn or tied into the garment, man wanders to another country, content with a little, friend later shows him.
'The aim of full awakening' stands for the aspiration to omniscience the arhats say the Buddha placed in them; confirm the plain wording.
'Some East Asian teachers later read the jewel as buddha-nature' is a general reception claim; confirm or cut.
Week-end look back pairs this parable with the lost son (ch. 4) and phantom city (ch. 7); confirm the framing.
Original: रत्न (ratna); the Sanskrit of the parable may use maṇi or maṇiratna. Confirm.
